title: Democratizing Foundations of Problem-Solving with AI: A Breadth-First Search Curriculum for Middle School Students
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of integrating AI education into existing subject-area instruction in ways that are feasible for K–12 classrooms and accessible to students without prior computing experience. The authors focus on teaching Breadth-First Search (BFS) as a concrete example of AI problem-solving, using it to help students understand representation and reasoning in AI while keeping the content connected to regular classroom science instruction.

The intervention was a co-designed seven-day curriculum implemented in a rural middle school health science course in the United States. It combined four simulation-based activities in an interactive Snap!-based environment called I-SAIL with unplugged tracing tasks, a hands-on virus-spread/contact-tracing activity, and science-based applications that linked BFS to contact networks and virus transmission. The study included six classrooms across grades 6–8, with data drawn from pre/post BFS assessments, student work artifacts, and a teacher interview.

Results showed statistically significant improvement in students’ BFS understanding from pre- to post-test, and most students could correctly identify the shortest path on an unplugged worksheet, though many still struggled to document the full step-by-step procedure. The teacher reported that the curriculum fit well within the science unit and helped students see both the AI and science relevance of the activities, while also suggesting the need for clearer language, more explicit vocabulary support, and additional teacher-facing scaffolds. Overall, the paper concludes that well-scaffolded, contextually grounded AI activities can broaden access to AI problem-solving within middle school science classes.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a classroom implementation study with pre/post assessment, student work artifacts, and a teacher interview, but it is not an RCT or quasi-experimental comparison with a control group. Evidence strength is therefore qualitative/mixed-methods and best classified as yellow.
impact_tier_rationale: The pre/post gain on BFS understanding is moderate (dz=0.453) in a priority K-12 population, indicating a modest-to-moderate positive impact. However, the study is small and lacks a comparison condition, so the overall impact should be treated as promising but not definitive.

interventions.use_case: interactive BFS learning environment (I-SAIL) with map-based graph tracing, scaffolded algorithm simulation, and unplugged/visual activities for middle school science-integrated AI problem-solving

finding.finding_summary: Students showed improved understanding of BFS and AI problem-solving after the curriculum. On the matched pre/post BFS assessment (n=41), scores increased from M=0.683 (SD=0.219) to M=0.790 (SD=0.232), a statistically significant gain with Cohen’s dz=0.453 (paired t(40)=2.90, p=.006; Wilcoxon W=87, p=.008).
finding.measure: Matched pre/post BFS knowledge assessment (5 multiple-choice items)

finding.finding_summary: Students were able to apply BFS in an unplugged worksheet after the core activities, with 64.5% accurately identifying the shortest path to the goal state. However, many still omitted intermediate steps and exploration-order details, indicating partial but emerging procedural understanding rather than fully consistent tracing skill.
finding.measure: Paper-based BFS tracing worksheet accuracy and completeness

finding.finding_summary: Teacher interview feedback indicated the curriculum supported student engagement and retention, especially through movement-based and interactive activities. The teacher reported that students were more likely to understand and recall material on days with active participation, suggesting a positive effect on engagement-related learning processes.
finding.measure: Teacher interview on engagement, retention, and classroom fit
